39.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, around 1446 B.C., when the Israelites left Egypt after centuries of slavery.
39.passage: Exodus 12 describes Passover, a key event marking the liberation of the Israelites, where God commands specific rituals to remember their deliverance.
39.culture: In Hebrew culture, unleavened bread is a symbol of purity and separation from sin, and Passover is celebrated each year to commemorate the deliverance from Egypt.
39.interpretation: This verse illustrates the haste with which God delivered His people, highlighting the urgency of responding to His call. Spiritually, it reminds us that our deliverance from the slavery of sin is immediate and requires our commitment.
39.commentaire: The fact that the Israelites left Egypt without provisions underscores their total dependence on God. Likewise, as Christians, we are called to shed our old habits and walk in faith, confident that God will provide for our spiritual needs. This passage encourages us to live a life of freedom, separating ourselves from anything that hinders our walk with Christ.

mots.sens: This word refers to a period of guard or watch. It is linked to the idea of protection and preservation. In the context of the Exodus, it emphasizes God's faithfulness to His people during their stay in Egypt, marking a time of preparation for their deliverance. Spiritually, it reminds believers that God watches over them even in times of trial.

Theologically, it evokes God's patience and His redemptive plan unfolding over the long term.

40.epoque: This verse is situated in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, around the 13th century B.C., a period marked by oppression and suffering of God's people.
40.passage: This passage is part of the Exodus narrative, where God announces the imminent liberation of His people after centuries of slavery. It underscores the fulfillment of divine promises and the preparation for deliverance.
40.culture: In Egyptian culture, time was often perceived as cyclical, but for the Israelites, this period of 430 years represents a time of suffering and purification, preparing their hearts for freedom.
40.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God is faithful to His promises, even when His people go through prolonged trials. It also shows that the time of suffering can be a means of preparation for divine deliverance.
40.commentaire: The stay of the Israelites in Egypt teaches us that even in times of distress, God has a plan for His people. This encourages us to trust in His faithfulness and sovereignty, knowing that He uses every period of our lives to prepare us for His work. As believers, we must maintain hope and faith, even when circumstances seem difficult.

mots.sens: This word means 'army' or 'host' and is often used to refer to military forces, but also to heavenly armies. In this context, it evokes the collective power of the Israelites, who are considered the army of the Lord. The theological significance of this term emphasizes that God's people are on a mission under His direction, illustrating the idea of divine deliverance and God's protection over His people.

This verb means 'to go out' or 'to exit.' It is often used in contexts of liberation or departure, and here, it marks the crucial moment of the exit from Egypt. This symbolizes not only a physical liberation but also a spiritual one, where the people are called to leave slavery and enter into the freedom that God has promised them.

This term refers to Egypt, a country that symbolizes oppression and slavery in the Bible. In the Exodus narrative, Egypt represents sin and servitude, while the exit from Egypt is a powerful metaphor for redemption. Spiritually, it reminds believers of their own exit from the slavery of sin through Christ.

The mention of 'four hundred thirty years' underscores God's faithfulness to His promises, even through prolonged periods of trial. It reminds believers that God is sovereign over time and that He acts according to His perfect plan.

41.epoque: This verse is situated in the context of the Exodus, which took place around the 13th century B.C., when the Israelites were liberated from Egyptian slavery under the leadership of Moses.
41.passage: In this chapter, God commands the Israelites to prepare for the Passover, marking the beginning of their liberation. The verse emphasizes the importance of the precise date of their exit, showing that God has a perfect plan and timing.
41.culture: Egyptian culture was marked by slavery and oppression, and the Exodus narrative represents a major turning point in Israel's history, symbolizing the transition from an oppressed people to a free nation under God's direction.
41.interpretation: This verse illustrates God's faithfulness to His people and the fulfillment of His promise of liberation. It also emphasizes that divine deliverance is often preceded by long periods of trial, but that God always acts at the right moment.
41.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God is faithful to His promises and that He delivers His people in His time. As believers, we must remember that even in times of waiting and trial, God is working for our good. We are called to come out of our own 'Egypts,' to leave behind sin and oppression, and to walk towards the freedom that Christ offers us.

mots.sens: This word means 'to celebrate' or 'to feast' and refers to an act of rejoicing in honor of God. It is often used to denote religious festivals in Jewish tradition, symbolizing joy and gratitude towards the Lord for His mighty acts. In this verse, it emphasizes the importance of remembering divine interventions in the history of the people of Israel.

This term means 'exit' or 'liberation' and evokes the idea of deliverance from a state of oppression. In the context of the Exodus, it refers to the exit from Egypt, a fundamental act of Israelite faith. Theologically, it represents liberation from sin and the promise of redemption through Christ.

This word means 'night' and often symbolizes a moment of transition or revelation in the Bible. The night of the Exodus is marked by God's power, who intervenes to save His people. Spiritually, it reminds us that even in darkness, God is present and active to deliver those who trust in Him.

42.epoque: This passage is situated in the context of the Exodus, around 1446 B.C., when the Israelites are liberated from slavery in Egypt, marking a major turning point in their history as God's chosen people.
42.passage: This verse is part of the instructions given by God to Moses regarding the Passover, a celebration that commemorates Israel's liberation from slavery. It emphasizes the importance of remembering that night when the Lord acted powerfully to save His people.
42.culture: In Israelite culture, festivals and celebrations are key moments for transmitting the identity and history of the people. The Passover is particularly significant, as it recalls not only physical liberation but also the covenant relationship between God and Israel.
42.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse reminds us of the importance of celebrating God's works in our lives. It invites us to recognize and honor the moments when God has delivered us, encouraging us to pass this memory on to future generations.
42.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of memory and celebration in our walk with God. By remembering His past works, we strengthen our faith and trust in His ability to act in our present. May every 'night' of our lives be an opportunity to celebrate the faithfulness of the Lord and to pass this truth on to our children.

mots.sens: The word 'Pésach' refers to Passover, a central event in the history of Israel. It comes from the verbal root 'pasach', which means 'to pass over' or 'to spare'. Theologically, Passover represents God's deliverance and protection of His people, symbolizing the transition from death to life, which finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ.

43.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, when the Israelites are about to leave Egypt after centuries of slavery, under the leadership of Moses and Aaron.
43.passage: In Exodus 12, God gives precise instructions regarding the celebration of Passover, marking Israel's liberation from Egyptian oppression. This chapter is crucial as it establishes the foundations of Israel's collective memory and religious rites.
43.culture: Passover is a Jewish celebration that commemorates liberation from slavery, surrounded by rituals and traditions that reinforce the national and spiritual identity of the people. The fact that only members of the people of Israel can participate in Passover underscores the importance of community and the covenant with God.
43.interpretation: The exclusion of strangers from Passover emphasizes the idea that communion with God and participation in His promises require an authentic relationship with Him. This reminds us that, in the New Testament, access to God is open to all, but through faith in Christ, who is our Passover.
43.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of belonging to God's community in order to receive His blessings. As Christians, we are called to celebrate our deliverance in Christ, our Passover, and to invite those who do not yet know this relationship to discover God's grace. This compels us to live our faith authentically and to share the Gospel with those who are still 'strangers' to God's promise.

mots.sens: This word means 'slave' or 'servant'. It designates a person who is under the authority of another, often due to debt or acquisition. In the biblical context, slavery can be seen as a metaphor for servitude to God, highlighting the idea of devotion and obedience. Spiritually, this reminds us that we are called to be servants of Christ, engaged in a relationship of dependence and faithfulness to Him.

This term means 'tomorrow' or 'the next day'. It evokes the idea of waiting and preparation for the future. This reminds us that, through faith in Christ, we are integrated into a new covenant.

44.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, when the Israelites are about to leave Egypt after centuries of slavery. It is a major transitional period for God's people, marked by miracles and divine judgments.
44.passage: Exodus 12 deals with Passover, a central event in the history of Israel, where God commands the Israelites to sacrifice a lamb and mark their doors to be spared from judgment. This chapter emphasizes the importance of obedience to God's commandments.
44.culture: In Hebrew culture, circumcision is a rite of initiation and a sign of covenant with God. It represents spiritual commitment and national identity, integrating individuals into the community of Israel.
44.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse emphasizes that all those under God's authority, even strangers or slaves, have access to the Lord's table. This foreshadows the inclusion of all nations in God's plan of salvation through Jesus Christ.
44.commentaire: This verse reminds us that God's grace is accessible to all, regardless of their social status. By circumcising the slave, God shows that everyone has a place in His people. As Christians, we must welcome all those who seek to know Christ, offering them a place at His table.

mots.sens: This word means 'man' or 'individual'. It evokes not only the notion of humanity but also interpersonal relationships and responsibilities. In the context of the Exodus, this underscores that the Passover sacrifice is not intended for those motivated by material interests, but for those who share a spiritual relationship with God.

45.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, when the Israelites are about to leave Egypt, a crucial moment in their history when God establishes laws and rites to define their identity as a chosen people.
45.passage: In Exodus 12, God institutes Passover, a central ritual that commemorates Israel's liberation from slavery. This verse specifies who may participate in this sacred meal, emphasizing the importance of belonging to the community of Israel.
45.culture: In Hebrew culture, the notion of community and belonging is paramount. Sacred rites are reserved for those who share the faith and identity of Israel, reflecting a broader understanding of the relationship between God and His people.
45.interpretation: This verse reminds us that communion with God and participation in sacred rites require spiritual belonging. The inhabitants and mercenaries, although physically present, cannot participate in Passover, symbolizing the importance of faith and commitment to God.
45.commentaire: This passage teaches us that true communion with God is reserved for those who are in relationship with Him. As Christians, we are called to reflect on our own belonging to the faith community and our commitment to Christ. This also invites us to consider how we welcome those who seek to know God while maintaining the purity of our faith.

mots.sens: This word means 'house' and evokes a place of refuge, safety, and community. It is often used in the Bible to symbolize the presence of God and the place where the people gather to worship. In this verse, the house becomes a sacred space where the Passover lamb is consumed, highlighting the importance of communion and unity in faith.

This verb means 'to break' or 'to shatter' and evokes the idea of destruction or separation. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the importance of preserving the integrity of the Passover lamb, a symbol of Christ, whose bones will not be broken. This anticipates the crucifixion of Jesus, where, despite the suffering, His body remained intact, affirming His perfection and complete sacrifice.

46.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, when the Israelites are about to leave Egypt after years of slavery. It is a pivotal moment in Israel's history, marked by divine deliverance and the establishment of the covenant between God and His people.
46.passage: In Exodus 12, God gives specific instructions regarding the Passover, an essential rite for the Israelites. The chapter describes how the Passover lamb is to be sacrificed and consumed, symbolizing divine protection against judgment, and this verse highlights important details about how this should be done.
46.culture: In Israelite culture, the house is not only a physical place but also a symbol of community and family. Religious rites, such as Passover, were often celebrated with family, reinforcing bonds and the collective memory of God's acts.
46.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of obedience to God's commandments, particularly in the context of the Passover sacrifice. Spiritually, it reminds us that our communion with Christ must be lived out in a community setting, and that we must respect the holiness of His sacrifice.
46.commentaire: This passage teaches us that communion with God is experienced in a context of closeness and obedience. By celebrating Passover, the Israelites were called to remember God's deliverance, just as we are called to remember Christ's sacrifice. By remaining in the 'house,' we find protection and unity, and we are invited to live out our faith in community, honoring the perfect sacrifice of Jesus.

mots.sens: The word 'Pessaḥ' means 'to pass over' or 'to spare.' It is derived from the Hebrew root that evokes the idea of protection and deliverance. Theologically, this foreshadows the sacrifice of Christ, who, by His blood, protects us from eternal death.

47.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, around 1446 B.C., when the Israelites are about to leave Egypt after centuries of slavery.
47.passage: Exodus chapter 12 describes the instructions given by God for the celebration of Passover, a significant event that symbolizes Israel's liberation and divine protection during the judgment on Egypt.
47.culture: In Hebrew culture, Passover is a central moment of memory and celebration, where each family gathers to commemorate the deliverance from slavery and God's faithfulness to His people.
47.interpretation: The instruction that 'the whole assembly of Israel shall keep the Passover' emphasizes the importance of unity and collective participation in worship. It reminds us that God's redemption and grace are offered to all who are part of His people.
47.commentaire: This verse teaches us that faith is not lived in isolation, but in community. By celebrating Passover together, the Israelites affirmed their identity as God's people, just as we, as Christians, are called to gather to celebrate our redemption in Christ. Passover invites us to reflect on our own commitment to the faith community and how we bear witness to God's grace in our lives.

mots.sens: This word means 'circumcision.' It is derived from the Hebrew root that evokes the idea of cutting or incising. Spiritually, it represents the necessity of purification and preparation to enter into communion with the Lord.

This term translates to 'stranger' or 'non-Jew.' It refers to a person who is not born into the people of Israel but lives among them. In the context of the covenant, it underscores the inclusivity of divine grace, allowing even strangers to participate in God's promises, provided they conform to spiritual requirements, such as circumcision.

This word means 'Passover,' a central event in Jewish tradition that commemorates Israel's liberation from slavery in Egypt. The term is related to the idea of 'passing over,' in reference to the divine protection over the houses marked with the blood of the lamb. Theologically, Passover foreshadows the sacrifice of Christ, the Lamb of God, who frees believers from the bondage of sin.

48.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, when the Israelites are preparing to leave Egypt, marking a major turning point in their history as God's chosen people.
48.passage: Exodus 12 deals with the instructions given by God for the celebration of Passover, an act of memory and faith that unites the people of Israel around their identity and divine liberation.
48.culture: In Israelite culture, circumcision is a fundamental initiation rite that symbolizes belonging to the community of Israel and the covenant with God, highlighting the importance of ritual purity.
48.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that access to God's promises and communion with Him is not limited to the descendants of Abraham alone. It shows that faith and obedience are essential for all, including those who are strangers, provided they conform to divine requirements.
48.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God's grace is accessible to all who commit to follow Him, regardless of their origins. It encourages us to welcome those who seek God into our community, while highlighting the importance of personal transformation and obedience to His commandments. Circumcision, as a symbol of commitment to God, invites us to examine our own hearts and ensure that we are spiritually 'circumcised' to fully participate in the life of faith.

mots.sens: The term 'Torah' literally means 'instruction' or 'law'. It refers to the entirety of the commandments and teachings given by God to the people of Israel. In this context, the Torah represents the divine will that must be respected by all, without distinction. This underscores the universality of God's law, which applies to all human beings, whether they are natives or foreigners.

The word 'Ezrach' refers to a citizen or native, implying belonging to the community. It indicates a person who has rights and responsibilities within society. Spiritually, this emphasizes that all who live in the community of faith are called to respect the same laws and principles, reinforcing the idea of equality before God.

The term 'Ger' designates a foreigner or a temporary resident. In Israelite culture, 'Gérim' were often people who chose to live among the people of Israel, adopting its laws and customs. This reminds us that welcoming and integrating foreigners are important values in the faith, highlighting God's mercy and justice toward all.

49.epoque: This verse comes from a time when the people of Israel were on their way to the promised land, after being freed from slavery in Egypt. It was a moment of identity formation and the establishment of divine laws for a nascent nation.
49.passage: Exodus 12 deals with the Passover, a central event in the history of Israel, marking their liberation. The chapter establishes precise instructions on how the Israelites were to celebrate this feast, emphasizing the importance of the law and obedience to God.
49.culture: In Israelite culture, the law was seen as a gift from God, governing not only spiritual life but also social relationships. The inclusion of foreigners in the law underscores the importance of social justice and equality in the community.
49.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God's law is not reserved for a particular group, but applies to all who choose to live under His authority. It highlights the inclusive nature of the kingdom of God, where every individual, regardless of their background, is called to live according to His precepts.
49.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of equality and unity in faith. As believers, we are called to welcome those who come among us and to live according to the same biblical principles. This challenges us to reflect on our attitude toward others and to promote a community where everyone is valued and respected, regardless of their origin.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to do' or 'to act'. It implies a concrete action, often in response to a divine command. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the importance of obedience and the fulfillment of the instructions given by God through Moses and Aaron, which is fundamental for the relationship between God and His people.

This word means 'to command' or 'to order'. It evokes the idea of an authority giving precise instructions. In this verse, it highlights the divine nature of the commandments, indicating that the obedience of the children of Israel is a response to God's authority, which is essential for faithfulness and communion with Him.

This expression means 'the children of Israel' and designates God's chosen people. It emphasizes the collective identity and responsibility of this people toward God's commandments. Spiritually, it reminds us that believers today are also called to be children of God, called to live according to His precepts.

50.epoque: This verse is situated in the context of the Exodus, a period when the Israelites were freed from slavery in Egypt, around the 13th century B.C.
50.passage: Chapter 12 of Exodus describes the preparation for the Passover, a significant event for the people of Israel, symbolizing their liberation and the establishment of a new identity as God's people.
50.culture: In Hebrew culture, obedience to God's commandments is essential and is often linked to the survival and blessing of the people. The celebration of the Passover is an act of memory and faith.
50.interpretation: This verse illustrates the response of the children of Israel to divine instruction, highlighting their obedience. Spiritually, it reminds us of the importance of listening to and following God's directives in our daily lives.
50.commentaire: The obedience of the children of Israel to what the Lord had commanded is a model for us today. As believers, we are called to act according to the word of God, thus demonstrating our faith through our actions. This verse encourages us to live a life of obedience, knowing that this brings us closer to God and allows us to participate in His redemptive plan.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to go out' or 'to exit'. It is often used to describe a physical or spiritual movement toward freedom or a new state. In the context of the Exodus, it symbolizes the deliverance from slavery and the entry into a new covenant with God. The theological significance of this word emphasizes the idea of divine liberation and a call to a new way of life in communion with the Lord.

This term designates Egypt, which is often seen as a symbol of oppression and idolatry. Etymologically, the word can be linked to concepts of confinement and limitation. Spiritually, Egypt represents the world and its systems that keep people in bondage, while the exit from Egypt is a metaphor for deliverance from sin and the transition to life in Christ.

This word means 'children' or 'sons'. In Hebrew culture, it carries a deep significance of heritage, continuity, and family relationship. Spiritually, it evokes the idea that the children of Israel are considered the sons of God, called to live according to His precepts and to bear witness to His glory in the world.

This term means 'army' or 'host', and can also denote order and organization. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that the children of Israel were organized into groups, ready to enter a new phase of their existence. Theologically, this can be understood as preparation for the conquest of the promised land, symbolizing the call to commitment and struggle for faith.

51.epoque: This verse is situated in the context of the Exodus, a major event in the history of Israel, which occurred around the 13th century B.C., when the Hebrew people were enslaved in Egypt.
51.passage: This passage is part of the account of the exit from Egypt, where God executes His plan of deliverance for the children of Israel, marking the end of their slavery and the beginning of their journey to the promised land.
51.culture: In Hebrew culture, the exit from Egypt is celebrated during Passover, an event that recalls the liberation from slavery and the importance of God's faithfulness to His people.
51.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse highlights God's power to liberate His people from oppression. It reminds us that God is faithful to His promises and that He guides His people toward freedom and new life.
51.commentaire: This verse is a powerful reminder of the deliverance that God offers to each of us. Just as the children of Israel were called to come out of slavery, we are also called to break free from the chains of sin and walk in the freedom that Christ has won for us. As believers, we must remember that God is always at work to liberate us and lead us to our spiritual inheritance.
